# Distinguishing blocking, deadlock and starvation

## Start with one representative question

[S01-Q027](#S01-Q027)

<p>When can blocking asynchronous code contribute to deadlock or ThreadPool starvation? How would you distinguish those explanations for a slow application?</p>

## One group objective and observable capabilities

<p>Diagnose lack of progress by distinguishing blocking, deadlock and ThreadPool starvation hypotheses.</p>

<ul>
<li>Trace a specific wait and its required continuation or worker.</li>
<li>Identify observations that discriminate the failure hypotheses.</li>
<li>Validate a targeted repair under representative concurrent load.</li>
</ul>

**Prerequisites**

- [Async execution, waiting and failure](dotnet-async-io.md)

<p>A blocked request is a symptom, not a complete diagnosis. Follow what it waits for and whether the required work can progress; that separates a waiting cycle from worker-capacity pressure or a slow dependency.</p>

### S01-Q027 · Failure cases

<p>When can blocking asynchronous code contribute to deadlock or ThreadPool starvation? How would you distinguish those explanations for a slow application?</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q027](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q027)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q027](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q027)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> When can blocking asynchronous code cause deadlocks or ThreadPool starvation?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Investigate progress, waiting and available workers. Deadlock and starvation are different hypotheses; a blocked call alone does not prove either diagnosis.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Discriminate failure hypotheses using runtime and request evidence.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State runtime, application context and blocking call; check official diagnostics guidance before relying on context or ThreadPool behavior.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Traces a specific dependency or waiting cycle and identifies distinguishing observations.</li>
<li>Proposes a targeted change and validates latency and throughput without merely increasing thread counts.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Claiming every .Result or .Wait call necessarily deadlocks in every application.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What evidence would make you investigate downstream latency instead?</li>
</ul>

</details>

## Combined production exercise — agent-added

<p>A hypothetical API slows sharply under concurrency and contains synchronous waits on asynchronous operations. State its runtime and context, draw the wait relationships, and propose runtime plus request observations. Design a targeted change and comparison run; explain which outcome would make you reject the initial diagnosis.</p>

## Short rubric — use only with an actual attempt

**Basic answer**

<p>Distinguishes the terms and supplies a plausible wait trace.</p>

**Senior answer**

<p>Uses evidence to discriminate causes and confirms the repair without universal context assumptions.</p>

**Still needs evidence**

<p>A .Result occurrence or a high latency graph alone cannot establish deadlock or starvation.</p>
